title: On tiptoe
hookLine: on tiptoe you can't stand firm; striding, you won't go far (Tao Te Ching 24)

cards: If you're standing, try this. If you're sitting, just imagine it. Rise up onto your toes, as high as you can.
For a second you're taller. Then the calves start to burn, the ankles wobble, and your arms go out looking for balance. You can't stay there, and you can't walk well like that either.

Come back down, and feel the whole foot take the floor again: heel, arch, toes. That's steadiness, and it cost nothing. Chapter twenty-four of the Tao Te Ching starts right there, with a person straining on their toes.

teach.b: First, tiptoe, not firm. In Legge's translation the chapter begins: "He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm." The extra height is borrowed, and it has to be paid back quickly.
Second, striding, not far. The next line says the same of walking. Whoever stretches their legs into long strides won't get far.
A person who lunges down the road wears out before someone who just walks. The chapter is about posture, but not only about feet.

Third, chapter twenty-two, in reverse. Two days ago, chapter twenty-two said the sage doesn't display himself, and so he shines; doesn't boast, and so his work counts. Chapter twenty-four turns the same lines inside out.
Whoever shows himself off isn't seen clearly. Whoever insists he's right doesn't stand out. Whoever boasts gets no credit.
Whoever is proud of himself doesn't last. Showing off is a kind of standing on tiptoe: you look taller, and you can't hold it.
Fourth, leftover food, a growth. Then a blunt image.

teach.h: HE WHO STANDS ON HIS TIPTOES DOES NOT STAND FIRM.
teach.b: To the Way, the chapter says, these straining habits are like leftover food, or a useless growth on the body, things people turn away from. So whoever has the Way doesn't stay in them.
It isn't a moral scolding so much as a diagnosis: the strain is extra. It weighs on you and gets you nowhere.

how: Some people who read the Tao Te Ching use chapter twenty-four as a check on themselves: when they notice strain or showing off, they come back to a plain, steady way of standing and working.

o: moving carefully because the path is dangerous
straining to look taller, which you can't hold long
standing quietly so you don't disturb anyone

s: chapter twenty-four is only advice about how to stand
it starts with feet, then turns to showing off, boasting and pride.
chapter twenty-four turns chapter twenty-two's lines about the sage inside out
twenty-two: he doesn't boast, so his work counts. twenty-four: whoever boasts gets no credit.
the chapter says long strides get you there faster
whoever stretches into long strides won't get far.

games.q: you want to look taller than you are, for a moment, in a crowd. chapter twenty-four is watching. what happens on tiptoe?
o: you can hold it as long as you need.
you can't stand firm, and you have to come down.
you grow into the extra height.
games.why: "he who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm." the height is borrowed, and the chapter says the same of showing off.

practice: Sit with both feet flat on the floor, and feel them there. Bring to mind one place where you're up on your toes, trying to look like you have it handled or pushing faster than things can go.
Don't solve it; let your weight come down into your feet, and ask what standing on the whole foot would look like there.

wordCard.voice: On tiptoe. Chapter twenty-four's picture of strain: taller for a moment, never firm, and a stride too long to last. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, qǐ zhě bù lì: one on tiptoe does not stand. The opening of Tao Te Ching 24.

carryVoice: Your line: flat feet. The extra height is borrowed; the whole foot costs nothing. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm
